To "program" something means to give it a set of instructions so that it behaves in a specific, predictable way. Think of it as shaping the future behavior of something — a machine, a device, a schedule, or even a person — by feeding it rules, commands, or repeated experiences in advance.

This single idea — giving instructions to shape future behavior — connects every different use of this verb.
Meaning 1: To write instructions for a computer or machine

This is the most well-known modern use. When you program a computer, you write precise instructions in a special language (like Python or JavaScript) that the computer reads and obeys, step by step, to perform a task.

"She programmed an app that tracks your water intake." "He spent the weekend programming a video game." "The engineers programmed the robot to sort packages on the conveyor belt."

The critical thing to understand here is that a computer is brutally literal — it does exactly what it is told, nothing more, nothing less. So programming means thinking through every single step carefully and writing it out without any ambiguity.

You can also program simpler devices, like a thermostat, a microwave, or a remote control. This doesn't always involve writing code — sometimes it just means entering specific settings. But the idea is the same: you are telling the machine what to do before it does it. "I programmed the thermostat to turn on at 7 AM." "She programmed her phone to go silent after 10 PM."
Meaning 2: To plan or schedule a series of events or content

To program can mean to plan, organize, and arrange a set of events, performances, shows, or content — especially in the world of television, radio, cinema, or arts.

"The festival director programmed 20 films over five days." "The radio station carefully programs its morning shows to attract commuters." "They programmed a blend of classical and contemporary works for the concert series."

Here, you are essentially writing a schedule — deciding what will happen, in what order, and at what time. It's the same core idea: you are laying out instructions for something to follow.
Meaning 3: To condition a person's mind or behavior

This is one of the most fascinating uses of the word, and it goes much deeper than computers or schedules. You can "program" a person — or be programmed yourself — in the sense that repeated experiences, upbringing, training, culture, or environment can shape how you automatically think, feel, or react, often without you even being aware of it.

Just like a computer follows its code without questioning it, a person who has been "programmed" in a certain way tends to respond automatically, almost on instinct.

"Children are programmed by their environment to accept certain beliefs without question." "Years of military training programmed him to stay calm under extreme pressure." "Society programs us to associate success with wealth." "She had been programmed from a young age to believe that asking for help was a sign of weakness."

This meaning often suggests deep conditioning that built up over time. It can be used neutrally — "his training programmed him to react fast" — or critically — "advertising programs people to want things they don't actually need."

You'll also see it used reflexively, meaning you deliberately do it to yourself: "You can program yourself to wake up early by building a consistent routine." "He programmed himself to stay positive by repeating certain thoughts every morning." Here it has an empowering, intentional quality — you are consciously reshaping your own automatic responses.

A very common pattern is the passive — to be programmed to do something. This implies that something or someone has been set up, designed, or conditioned to behave a certain way — often by an external force.

"The machine is programmed to shut down automatically if it overheats." "We seem to be programmed to fear the unknown." "Bees are programmed by nature to return to the hive."

This passive form is especially common when describing instincts, biology, or deep conditioning — things that were essentially "installed" from outside, often long before the person or creature had any say in it.
What ties all these meanings together

Whether you're talking about a computer, a thermostat, a TV schedule, or a human mind — "to program" always involves three things:

A source of instructions (a coder, a planner, a culture, a repeated experience). Something that receives those instructions (a computer, a device, a broadcast schedule, a person). A resulting behavior that is predictable and consistent.

Programming is always about shaping how something will behave — before it actually behaves. The instructions come first; the behavior follows.

program + something + to + verb — "She programmed the robot to lift boxes." This is the most classic pattern: you give something instructions tied to a specific action.

program + something + for + time or setting — "Program the oven for 200 degrees." Here you're configuring a device for a specific condition.

be programmed + to + verb — "We are programmed to seek comfort." The passive form, often used for instincts, conditioning, or factory-set device behavior.

program yourself + to + verb — "Program yourself to focus for 25 minutes at a time." A deliberate, self-directed use, usually about building habits or mental conditioning.

What makes "program" such a rich and powerful word is that it quietly implies that behavior is not always spontaneous or free. Whether it's a machine or a human, something that has been "programmed" is following instructions — laid down in the past — that now run almost automatically. This is why the word is used both in computer science and in psychology, and why it can feel both clinical and deeply philosophical depending on the context.
